$comment: AZURE FRONT DOOR (Premium) + WAF - the sole public edge.
Front Door is not optional (ADR-002, spec 2657). It is the only public DNS name and the only
public IP this platform has; APIM and both backends are private. A request that did not come
through here did not come from a client.
Placeholders in ${...} are substituted by the deployment pipeline. Nothing here is a secret.
The Front Door id below is an identifier, not a credential - it is checked at APIM to make the
origin specific to this platform, and its value being known to an attacker buys nothing while
the network control also holds. That is what 'neither control is sufficient alone' means in
practice (spec 10.3): each one is weak in a different direction.
Premium rather than Standard for one reason that matters here: Private Link to the APIM origin.
Standard cannot reach a private origin, which would force APIM to hold a public endpoint and
would reduce the first hop's network control to an IP-range filter.

profile.name: synthia-edge
profile.$comment: frontDoorId is emitted by the deployment and bound into the APIM named value `front-door-id`. The two MUST be the same value; build/scripts/check-edge-path.sh asserts the APIM policy reads that named value rather than a literal.

originGroups.name: apim
$comment: EXACTLY ONE ORIGIN GROUP, pointing at exactly one origin: APIM. There is no second route
to a backend, no 'internal' endpoint and no bypass for health. A backend origin added here
would be a path around the trust boundary that looks, in the portal, like a routing entry.

healthProbe.$comment: APIM's own built-in status endpoint. It reports the gateway, not an application, so it neither traverses nor bypasses the identity boundary.

sharedPrivateLinkResource.requestMessage: Front Door to APIM, the only origin path.
sharedPrivateLinkResource.$comment: Private Link, so APIM has no public ingress at all. This is the network half of the frontdoor-to-apim hop in build/policy/edge-trust.json; the X-Azure-FDID check in build/infra/apim/global.inbound.xml is the application half.

routes.name: api
$comment: ONE PATTERN, and it is the audience prefix set. /api/customer/v1, /api/staff/v1 and
/api/workload/v1 all match; nothing else does. A wildcard /* here would publish whatever
APIM happens to expose today and whatever it is given tomorrow.
Caching is deliberately absent. Every response on these paths is tenant-scoped, and a
shared edge cache keyed on URL is a cross-tenant leak waiting for two callers to request
the same path (constitution Principle: tenant isolation at every layer).

policySettings.$comment: Prevention, not Detection. Detection mode is a WAF that writes reports about the attack it allowed through.

customRules.name: RateLimitPerClient
customRules.$comment: A ceiling, not the authorization control. APIM rate-limits again per caller, and neither is a substitute for the other: this one bounds an anonymous flood before it costs gateway capacity.

customRules.name: BlockSelfAssertedIdentityHeaders
$comment: DEFENCE IN DEPTH, AND NOTHING MORE. APIM deletes every inbound copy of the contract
unconditionally, so this rule is not what makes spoofing fail - it is what makes an
ATTEMPT visible at the outermost layer, in the WAF log, before it has consumed anything
further in.
It matches one header rather than all five on purpose. A caller forging identity sends
the tenant; matching the whole set here would duplicate, in a place nobody reviews
alongside the policy, a list whose single authoritative copy is edge-trust.json.
This rule MUST NOT be relied on as the anti-spoofing control. If APIM's deletion were
ever removed, a request with only X-Idp-Roles would pass here and reach a backend.
